title: The stone under the rice
hookLine: a plate heaped with rice, and a stone hidden under it: the Kashmiri poet Lal Ded, and the one word her teacher gave her
carry: the guru's one word: turn within
last: A SHARANA TAKES REFUGE IN GOD ALONE.

lines: THE BRIDE WHO BECAME LAL DED.
cards: Dinner is served, and the young wife's plate looks generous, a full mound of rice.
Only she knows what's underneath: a stone, with the rice spread thin over it, so the plate looks full while there's hardly anything to eat.

Kashmiris tell this story about a young bride named Lalla and the mother-in-law who, tradition says, served her this way. She doesn't complain. She eats what there is, washes the stone, and sets it back.
In time she would leave that house and become the poet Kashmir remembers as Lal Ded.

teach.b: She goes by more than one name: Lalla, Lalleshwari, and Lal Ded, the one Kashmir knows best.
She sang in Kashmiri, not Sanskrit, in short sayings called vakhs, easy to remember and pass from mouth to mouth.
The stories say that after years of hardship at home she walked out as a wandering seeker, and found a teacher. Then comes a saying about that teacher, in paraphrase.
My teacher gave me only one word. He said: from outside, go within. That one word became my rule, and so I began to dance, with nothing on.
Notice how little she was given. Not a library, not a long course of rituals. One word.

That's still how many Hindus receive a path: from a guru, at initiation, diksha, often as one short word or mantra, given in person and kept for life. And she didn't argue with it or add to it. She took it all the way.

If what matters is within, then the outside, even the clothes, stops being the point. The stone story fits: a plate that looks full and isn't, and a bride who keeps quiet, because what feeds her isn't on the plate.
Some readers hear her saying as a teaching about Shiva, found inside, the way some Shaiva teachers in Kashmir speak of him. This season, four days with her, starting with the one word.

how: Lal Ded's vakhs are recited and sung in Kashmiri, quoted in everyday speech, and remembered by Kashmiris of more than one faith.

o: a Sanskrit scholar who wrote commentaries on the Gita
a Kashmiri poet-saint who sang short sayings called vakhs
a Kashmiri queen remembered for building Shiva temples

games.q: the bride who became Lal Ded — tap the pairs.
p: hidden under a thin layer of rice

s: Lal Ded sang in Sanskrit, the language of the old scriptures
she sang in Kashmiri, in short sayings called vakhs.
in her saying, her teacher gave her a long course of rituals
he gave her one word: from outside, go within.
in the story, Lalla didn't complain about the stone under the rice
she ate what there was, washed the stone and set it back.

games.q: you're Lalla. after years of hardship you find a teacher, and he gives you one word: from outside, go within. what do you do with it?
o: ask him for a longer course.
make it your rule and live it all the way.
games.why: she made that one word her rule and took it all the way; her vakh says it set her dancing free.

practice: Notice where your attention points right now: at sounds, at the screen, at the next thing to do.
Then gently turn it around, from outside in, and feel the breath at the tip of the nose, then in the chest; when the mind runs back outside, and it will, turn it in again.
If you have a mantra from a teacher or your family, say it silently there. If you pray, look for God within, in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Lal Ded. The Kashmiri poet whose teacher gave her one word, from outside, go within, and who took it all the way. Today's word.

orig.note: Lalleshwari, a name for Lal Ded, here written in Devanagari.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru's one word, turn within. One word was enough, taken all the way. See you tomorrow.
